summary: 2 detectors ran on sub-01 (None, run 01), 60 s of recording, 50 channels. Highest event rate: AR2-AR3 (rms 90.0/min, line_length 65.0/min). 1 of the leading channels are ranked very differently by the two detectors. This report presents evidence windows and rates; it contains no diagnosis and no recommendation.

disagreements.note: the two detectors' ranks differ by 6 places; the report states both and resolves neither

rms: 82 of 1121 accepted events (7%) coincide with an interictal discharge on the same channel — 82.0/min against 1039.0/min for the rest, summed over all channels. The two are reported separately because nothing here can tell a physiological ripple from an epileptic one, and merging them hides that.

line_length: 78 of 641 accepted events (12%) coincide with an interictal discharge on the same channel — 78.0/min against 563.0/min for the rest, summed over all channels. The two are reported separately because nothing here can tell a physiological ripple from an epileptic one, and merging them hides that.

Discharge co-occurrence is a proxy for the physiological/epileptic distinction, not a label for it: no public archive marks which ripples were physiological, so neither sub-population should be read as one or the other.
All 43 contacts passed the quality checks.

limitations: prototype: thresholds come from the literature, checked on synthetic data and against expert markings on 20 subjects of ds003498; not validated on a clinical cohort

this recording carries expert HFO markings, so the detectors can be scored on it (python -m onset_hfo.cli benchmark); agreement with those markings is not accuracy, because the reference is another detector's validated output
event rate is not a diagnosis: physiological ripples occur in healthy tissue, particularly in mesial temporal and occipital regions
a single short window of a single patient; nothing here generalises
bipolar pairs are formed from consecutive contact numbers, which on a grid is not always spatial adjacency
